results.q: How did the workers end up opening the wrong flange at PEMEX?
results.text:
They ended up opening the wrong flange because PEMEX did not give them a clear, standardized way to identify the exact equipment for opening. The boilermakers were looking for the blind location by using orange-and-blue blind tags and, more often, unlocked flange-locking devices instead of the blind list and drawing, because those job aids did not clearly show the right location. [pemex-012][pemex-018][pemex-019]

In the field, they saw an unlocked flange-locking device on the ARU7 piping. That device was not meant to identify what to open, but they treated it as a signal that this was the Blind 407 location. That led them to choose an active line instead of the intended, isolated ARU6 line. [pemex-019][pemex-020]

The problem was made worse because the Blind 407 tag was not placed directly on the flange and was out of sight, and PEMEX had no standardized process for flange opening and blind removal. The CSB said the workers relied on improvised markers because the written system and markings were ineffective. [pemex-019][pemex-025][pemex-046]

results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
The furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca was caused by the inadvertent simultaneous opening of both motor-operated valves that isolated Furnace 5. That created a path for cracked gas to backflow into the furnace’s firebox, where it built up and was then ignited by an existing flame. [monaca-037][monaca-015][monaca-016]

Several factors contributed. Shell assigned a process control engineer with limited process knowledge to manipulate the valves. Shell also relied on ineffective administrative controls instead of engineered safeguards to prevent the backflow hazard. [monaca-037][monaca-001] The control screen used to open the valves also made human error more likely because it showed the valves together on one diagram without clear labels to distinguish them. [monaca-037][monaca-002]

In short: the valves were opened in a way that unintentionally connected a higher-pressure gas source to the furnace, gas accumulated in the firebox, and the lit pilots ignited it. [monaca-015][monaca-016]

results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
The furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca was caused by the inadvertent simultaneous opening of two motor-operated valves used to isolate Furnace 5. That created a path for cracked gas to backflow into the furnace firebox, where lit pilots ignited it and caused the explosion. [monaca-037]

Several things contributed to it. Shell assigned a process control engineer with limited process knowledge to handle the valves, relied on administrative controls instead of an engineered safeguard against backflow, and used a human-machine interface that put three similar valves on one screen without clear labels, which increased the chance of error. [monaca-037][monaca-002]

In the incident sequence, cracked gas from the higher-pressure header backflowed into Furnace 5 for about 2.5 minutes, accumulated in the firebox, and then ignited. The furnace was not designed to contain an internal explosion. [monaca-015][monaca-016]

The consequences were severe: the explosion released hazardous chemicals, caused substantial property damage, evacuated 15 employees, and Shell estimated about $95 million in damage. [monaca-017][monaca-001]

results.q: What did the CSB recommend to Shell Polymers?
results.text:
For Shell Polymers Monaca, the CSB recommended two things to Shell Polymers Monaca itself:

1. Review the ethane cracking unit process hazard analysis to find process deviations that are handled only by administrative controls, and then add an inherently safer design or an engineered control for any scenario that could lead to a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage. [monaca-038]

2. Based on licensor input and good industry practices, implement and maintain an engineered control to prevent cracked gas from flowing back into a furnace during all modes of furnace operation. [monaca-038]

The report also says Shell had already made some corrective changes after the incident, so the CSB was not making recommendations on those exact issues. But it urged Shell to make sure the new controls are fully implemented and consistently followed across all furnaces, and to clean the furnace coke traps periodically in line with Linde’s guidance. [monaca-038]

In plain terms: the CSB wanted Shell to replace weak, procedure-based protections with stronger engineered safeguards, especially for scenarios that could cause a major fire or explosion. [monaca-038]

results.q: What mechanical integrity problems did the CSB find in the 2023 Honeywell reboiler explosion?
results.text:
The CSB found that Honeywell’s mechanical integrity system failed to manage a known reboiler shell deficiency to safe resolution. In October 2021, Honeywell’s own inspection found the shell had less than one year of remaining useful life and needed replacement, but the site did not document that deficiency in SAP or DMAPS, did not create a notification for the next inspection, and did not keep the issue visible to operations, maintenance, and reliability personnel. [geismar-028][geismar-031]

The report also says the site did not fully communicate the problem to other key stakeholders after the inspection, and that the MI functions were siloed. That meant the people who could have ensured replacement did not have the information they needed. [geismar-034][geismar-031]

The CSB further found that Honeywell did not preserve critical thickness data or fully investigate earlier shell-correlation problems from the reboiler’s history, including earlier shell failures and inconclusive corrosion-rate questions. [geismar-024][geismar-025][geismar-026]

After the January 23, 2023 failure, metallurgical examination found the shell had severely thinned from HF corrosion, with some locations down to 0.030 inches, about 95% thickness loss. [geismar-028]

results.q: Why was Reactor 6's relief system inadequate at Givaudan?
results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was too small for the runaway reaction that developed. The system itself did not appear to be mechanically broken; it opened when pressure got high. But the CSB concluded it was undersized for the accelerated sugar decomposition reaction, so it could not relieve gas and pressure fast enough. [givaudan-034][givaudan-035]

The relief setup on Reactor 6 used a 4-inch rupture disc and a 4M6 pressure relief valve in series, with the valve outlet tied into 6-inch piping. The CSB’s modeling found that, to prevent rupture, the system would have needed to be about four times larger, or a 4-inch rupture disc alone could have provided enough relief capacity. [givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

Because the relief system could not keep up, the pressure in Reactor 6 kept rising until the reactor ruptured. [givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

results.q: Why was Reactor 6's relief system inadequate at Givaudan?
results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was too small for the runaway reaction that developed. The system did open when pressure rose, but it could not remove gas and pressure fast enough, so the reactor kept pressurizing until it ruptured. [givaudan-019][givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

The CSB said the relief system on Reactor 6 was based on Reactor 2’s design, but the facility had no documentation showing the design basis for Reactor 2’s emergency relief system. Reactor 6 had a rupture disc and a pressure relief valve in series, with relief piping to a catch tank and then to the scrubber system. [givaudan-033]

The key problem was sizing. The CSB concluded the relief system functioned as designed, but was undersized for the accelerated sugar decomposition reaction that occurred that day. Because of that, the gases and pressure generated by the reaction could not be adequately relieved. [givaudan-033][givaudan-060]

The CSB’s modeling found that preventing rupture would have required a pressure relief valve with at least 16.74 square inches of relief area, about four times the capacity of the installed 4M6 valve. As an alternative, a 4-inch rupture disc alone could have provided enough relief capacity. [givaudan-035]

In short, the system was not failed mechanically; it was too small for the event it had to handle. [givaudan-034][givaudan-060]

results.q: What was the means-of-egress problem in the Wacker incident?
results.text:
The means-of-egress problem was that the fifth-floor platform had only a single staircase exit. When the hydrogen chloride cloud formed, the workers could not clearly see or safely reach that staircase, so the three workers without full chemical-resistant suits tried to climb down piping instead. One fell 70 feet and was killed, and two others were seriously injured. [wacker-001][wacker-013]

Wacker’s own process hazard analysis had already identified the risk of only one exit and had recommended a second route, such as a caged ladder on the opposite end of the structure, if the path to the stairs was blocked. But no secondary egress was installed before the incident. [wacker-027][wacker-033]

The CSB concluded that Wacker’s limited means of egress from the equipment access structure contributed to the severity of the event, and that current building requirements did not provide sufficient egress from elevated work platforms used to access hazardous materials. [wacker-034][wacker-032]

results.q: Which incidents involved problems with pressure relief systems?
results.text:
From the six reports, the incident that clearly involved a pressure relief system problem was Dow Louisiana Operations. Its product cooler had an emergency pressure-relief system made up of a rupture disc and a PRV, and Dow routed that relief piping to the reflux drum. The CSB found that this design contributed to the severity of the incident because ethylene oxide ignited in the pressure relief piping, the PRV lifted, and the hot material then overpressured the reflux drum and caused it to fail catastrophically [dow-006][dow-012][dow-031]. The report also says the pressure relief piping between the rupture disc and PRV lost its inert nitrogen atmosphere, which let air enter the piping and allowed ignition [dow-025][dow-031].

The Givaudan Sense Colour report also involves an emergency pressure relief system, but the CSB said the system functioned as designed. The problem there was that the relief system was undersized for the runaway reaction, so it could not relieve pressure fast enough and Reactor 6 ruptured [givaudan-033][givaudan-035].

The other three reports do not describe a pressure relief system failure as a main issue: PEMEX Deer Park was about the wrong equipment being opened and a hydrogen sulfide release [pemex-048], Shell Polymers Monaca was about wrong valve operation and a fire/explosion path [monaca-037], and Wacker Polysilicon was about over-torquing a flange on HCl piping [wacker-034].

results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
They have a lot in common in how they went wrong.

In both incidents, workers were doing maintenance on operating equipment, and the key failure was that the wrong risk controls were used for the job. At PEMEX, workers opened the wrong piping, which released pressurized hydrogen sulfide because the equipment was not clearly identified and the work permit did not adequately control the hazard [pemex-048][pemex-032]. At Wacker, contractors over-torqued bolts on live HCl piping, which cracked equipment and released gaseous hydrogen chloride, and Wacker did not have written procedures or enough control of hazardous energy for the task [wacker-034][wacker-001].

Both reports also point to weak control of simultaneous work. At PEMEX, the flange-opening work was done in an active unit next to a turnaround area with many other contractors nearby [pemex-048][pemex-003]. At Wacker, torquing work happened at the same time as unrelated insulation work on the same platform, and Wacker did not have a formal SIMOPs process to manage that overlap [wacker-001][wacker-033].

A second common theme is that both incidents exposed workers who were not part of the task itself. PEMEX’s release harmed workers in adjacent areas and triggered shelter-in-place orders [pemex-001]. Wacker’s release unnecessarily exposed other contractors on the platform, and the single staircase made escape difficult [wacker-002][wacker-033].

In short: both were maintenance incidents where poor identification, weak permitting, and poor coordination of simultaneous work made a routine job become a serious toxic release [pemex-017][wacker-033].

results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
They have a few important things in common.

Both incidents involved **contract workers doing maintenance on live process equipment** and the work went wrong because the job was not controlled well enough before it started. In PEMEX, workers opened the wrong piping and released toxic hydrogen sulfide. In Wacker, a contractor over-torqued bolts on an HCl piping flange and broke the equipment, releasing hydrogen chloride gas. [pemex-001][wacker-001]

In both cases, the CSB pointed to **weak work planning and work permitting**. PEMEX’s permit was too broad and did not control the hazards of opening piping in an operating unit. Wacker’s safe work permit did not properly address the risk of torquing on equipment containing hazardous energy. [pemex-002][wacker-018]

Both reports also stress **the need to clearly identify and control hazards before work begins**. PEMEX lacked a reliable way to identify the correct piping to open. Wacker lacked written, job-specific torquing procedures and did not do a risk analysis before the work. [pemex-017][wacker-033][wacker-018]

Finally, in both incidents, **other workers were put in danger because the hazard spread beyond the task crew**. PEMEX exposed workers in a nearby unit. Wacker exposed workers from a separate contractor crew who were working nearby. [pemex-002][wacker-002]

So the shared lesson is: if you do maintenance near operating equipment, you need clear identification, job-specific procedures, and permits that actually control the hazards. [pemex-050][wacker-022]

results.q: What's the best way to size a pressure relief valve?
results.text:
For a pressure relief valve, the best practice is to size it for the actual overpressure scenario you are protecting against, not just to match a valve on similar equipment. In the Givaudan report, the CSB found the Reactor 6 relief system was “based on that of Reactor 2,” but the facility had no documentation showing the design basis for Reactor 2’s relief system. The result was an undersized system for the runaway reaction that occurred. [givaudan-033]

The report says the owner/operator is responsible for determining all potential overpressure scenarios and the method of protection for each one. [givaudan-033] It also says the relief system must have enough capacity to lower pressure fast enough to keep the equipment below its design limits; otherwise rupture can occur. [givaudan-033]

For Reactor 6, the CSB’s modeling found that a PRV alone would have needed at least 16.74 square inches of relief area to provide the needed protection. [givaudan-035] That was more than four times the capacity of the 4M6 valve installed. [givaudan-035] The study also found that the existing 4-inch rupture disc alone could have provided enough relief capacity. [givaudan-035]

So the practical answer is: define the credible upsets, calculate the required relief capacity for each one, and then size the valve and connected piping to meet that demand. If the system is a PRV plus rupture disc, both devices and the piping between them have to be part of the sizing basis. [givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

results.q: What did the CSB conclude about the Evergreen Packaging incident?
results.text:
The CSB concluded that the incident was caused by metal debris puncturing a rupture disc and letting ethylene oxide get into piping that contained air. The ethylene oxide ignited, burned through the pressure relief piping, and reached a reflux drum filled with ethylene oxide. That made the drum overpressurize and fail catastrophically. [dow-032]

The CSB also said Dow’s vessel closure practices were inadequate. Work lights were left in the reflux drum during the turnaround, then degraded and broke apart, and the debris moved downstream. That debris was what likely damaged the rupture disc. [dow-031][dow-009]

Two other major contributors were Dow’s failure to keep the pressure relief piping inert and its lack of requirements to make sure the piping stayed inert during operation. [dow-032][dow-027]

The CSB said the severity was worsened by the system design, because the product cooler’s emergency pressure relief discharged back into the reflux drum. If the product cooler had been designed so pressure relief was not needed, the consequences would have been greatly reduced. [dow-032]
